name: Redness-minimizing ring light

lead: A ring light is a circular LED lamp that surrounds a camera so the face is lit evenly from all sides. Creators use it for selfies, makeup videos and streaming to look clearer-skinned and brighter-eyed on camera.

Light arrives almost along the camera axis from all around, so shadows are filled in, skin texture looks smoother, and the eyes get a ring-shaped catchlight. Adjustable colour temperature changes how warm or cool skin appears. This is an effect in photos and video only, and no study has tested redness reduction specifically.

paras: People mount the ring around a phone or camera at face height, pick a colour temperature that suits their skin tone, and shoot straight on. It is used in selfies, content creation and video calls.
No safety concerns are documented beyond ordinary advice about bright light. The effect exists only while the light is used and depends on camera settings.

chain: Clearer skin and brighter eyes on camera
angle.text: A ring light fills in shadows, evens out skin tone and adds a catchlight that makes the eyes look brighter on camera, with adjustable colour temperature to tune the tone. The lighting effect is visible at once; its effect on redness specifically has not been tested.

lead: A ring light is a circular light, usually a ring of LEDs, that sits around a camera lens or phone and lights the face from nearly all sides. People use one when taking selfies, photos and video so that skin looks even, shadows are minimal and the eyes pick up a bright ring-shaped catchlight [1][2]. A "redness-minimizing" setup refers to choosing the ring's color temperature and brightness so skin tone and the whites of the eyes look more even and less red on camera.

Because the light comes from the same direction as the lens, shadows fall behind the subject and are largely hidden. Descriptions say this reduces the appearance of skin texture and blemishes and gives a smoother look [1]. Consumer LED rings usually have adjustable brightness and color temperature, commonly from warm (about 3000 K) to cool (about 6000 K), and sellers highlight a high color rendering index for natural-looking skin tones [1].

Wikipedia notes that LED ring lights have become popular for video calls, selfies and vlogging, and that makeup artists also use them [2]. No published trial or measurement study has tested ring lights for reducing the visible redness of skin or eyes in photos.
infobox: LED ring (older designs used fluorescent tubes)

paras: Consumer ring lights are LED rings with adjustable brightness and color temperature, often sold with a tripod and a phone holder at the center [1]. Quality units are described as spanning roughly 3200 K (warm, tungsten-like) to 5600 K (daylight) and, in many models, a color rendering index of 95 or higher [1].
Continuous ring lights give steady, lower-intensity light than the brief burst of a ring flash, which suits video and previewing a shot [2].

The ring flash, the ancestor of the ring light, is credited by Grokipedia to dental photographer Lester Dine in 1952, for shadow-free pictures inside the mouth, and later spread to macro, fashion and forensic photography [1]. Wikipedia describes ring flashes as valued in portrait and fashion work for reducing shadows and creating a circular catchlight in the eyes [2].
Continuous LED ring lights followed in the 2000s and became popular from the mid-2010s among makeup creators, vloggers and streamers, with a further rise during the COVID-19 pandemic [1][2].

A ring flash surrounds the lens so light comes from almost the same direction the camera points, which keeps shadows minimal, and the effect is stronger for close subjects because the ring's size lets light reach the subject from many angles [2]. The ring shape creates a circular catchlight in the eyes [1][2].

Color temperature is measured in kelvins. Lower values give warmer yellow-to-red light and higher values give cooler, bluish light, and white balance settings correct for the difference [3]. Any effect on perceived redness depends on the setting chosen, brightness, camera white balance and the subject's skin tone; no published measurement quantifies this.

The idea appears in looksmaxxing lists on the basis that lighting makes skin look more even and the eyes look brighter in photos. Users apply it mainly for dating-profile pictures, social media and video, where even frontal light is the goal.
